newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam war architect returns to make peace.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam war architect returns to make peace.

text.p: Former U.S. defence secretary Robert McNamara, architect of America's involvement in the Vietnam War, began a series of meetings in Hanoi with his former foes on Thursday aimed at learning lessons from history.

McNamara, who last visited Vietnam in 1995 just months after the two countries normalised diplomatic ties, arrived on Wednesday and was due to lead a U.S. delegation in a conference over the coming weekend on missed opportunities.
But while he was received cordially ahead of that event, by officials including former foreign minister Nguyen Co Thach, signs were emerging that his mission might not be easy.

Conference organisers said they had not been told the reasons for a one-day delay to the event. McNamara's chief Vietnamese interlocutor, military mastermind General Vo Nguyen Giap, was scheduled to be absent from all but a closing session.

Reporters were meanwhile told Vietnamese officials taking part were unlikely to be available for either interview or comment, and Thursday's official Nhan Dan newspaper carried a commentary cricitising Washington for its policy towards Cuba.
But if the former U.S. defence chief was concerned, he wasn't showing it.
"I woudn't be here unless I thought we could add to history," he said in a doorstep interview outside his Hanoi hotel.
"I don't think either Vietnam or the U.S., or in a sense the world fully understands what happened. That's why we're here to explore it so it won't happen again."
McNamara, 81, a former Ford Motors executive, served as U.S. defence secretary under the Kennedy and Johnson administrations until 1968.

In a biography published in 1995 he sparked controversy by describing the decision-making process by which the United States escalated its involvement in the Vietnam war as having been "terribly wrong".
The conflict ended in April 1975 when the forces of communist North Vietnam overran Saigon. The cost in terms of human lives was 58,000 Americans and some three million Vietnamese.

McNamara said this week's conference would focus on the motives for each side in participating in the war as well as specific decisions and general principles held by each side at the time of the conflict.
However, he said the prime reason for holding the event was to promote the chances for future peace.

"It was a very, very costly conflict in terms of lives lost, and surely as you approach the 21st century the world should wish to try to avoid those conflicts," he said. "The question is how did this one come about, how could it have been avoided, how could future conflicts be avoided."
